title: The mole triangle: mass, particles, gas volume

blocks.text: Moles (n) are the bridge. Convert everything to moles first, use the equation's mole ratio, then convert back.

items: Mole ratio = ratio of coefficients in the BALANCED equation (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: H₂ : NH₃ = 3 : 2).
Mass of one molecule = M / Nₐ (one H₂O ≈ 18 / 6.02 × 10²³ ≈ 3 × 10⁻²³ g).

blocks.text: Coefficients give mole (and gas volume) ratios, never mass ratios. Balance first, then read the ratio.
Finding the limiting reactant

items: Divide the moles of each reactant by its coefficient.
The smallest answer is the limiting reactant: it runs out first and fixes the maximum product.
Excess left = amount taken − amount used by the limiting reactant.

blocks.text: Yield
% yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100. Theoretical yield is calculated from the limiting reactant; actual yield is what you really collect.

items: Actual = % yield × theoretical ÷ 100
Theoretical = actual × 100 ÷ % yield

blocks.text: Actual < theoretical because of side reactions, incomplete (reversible) reactions and losses while handling. A yield above 100% means the product is impure or still wet.

head: Feature
Positive (canal) rays
Cathode rays
rows: Towards the cathode, through its holes
Depends on the gas; largest for H₂ (H⁺)

blocks.text: Proton: charge +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, about 1836 times the electron's mass.
Positive rays are made by electrons knocking electrons off gas atoms, so they come from the gas, not from the anode metal.

title: Photons and the Bohr hydrogen atom

items: Photon energy: E = hν = hc/λ = hc·ν̄ (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
Wave number ν̄ = 1/λ, so E ∝ ν and E ∝ 1/λ: double λ, halve E
Bohr's allowed orbits: mvr = nh/2π
Radius rₙ = 0.529 n² Å (n = 2 → 2.12 Å)
Energy Eₙ ∝ −1/n²; gaps shrink as n rises
Emitted line: ΔE = E₂ − E₁ = hν (electron falls to a lower orbit)

blocks.text: The series is named by the LOWER level the electron lands on. Bohr's model works only for hydrogen and one-electron ions (He⁺, Li²⁺).

items: Aufbau: lowest (n + l) fills first; if equal, lower n first (4s before 3d).
Pauli: one orbital holds at most 2 electrons, opposite spins.
Hund: degenerate orbitals fill singly with parallel spins before pairing (O has 2 unpaired).

blocks.text: Exceptions: Cr = [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹, Cu = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (half-filled and full d are extra stable). Ions lose 4s before 3d: Fe²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁶, Fe³⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁵.
STP: 273 K (0 °C) and 1 atm = 760 mm Hg = 760 torr = 101325 Pa. One mole occupies 22.4 dm³.
Absolute zero: 0 K = −273.15 °C (often rounded to −273 °C). Charles: V changes by 1/273 of its 0 °C volume per °C.
Always use kelvin in Charles and ideal gas sums. Doubling 100 °C does not double V; doubling 100 K does.

title: Values of the gas constant R

head: Value of R
Units
rows: J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (= N m K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

blocks.text: Origin: R = PV/nT = (1 atm × 22.4 dm³) ÷ (1 mol × 273 K) = 0.0821. Physically, R is work done per mole per kelvin.
R is the same for every gas; only its number changes with the units. Converting: × 760 gives mm Hg, × 1000 gives cm³, ÷ 4.184 turns joules into calories.

title: Kinetic theory and why real gases deviate

blocks.text: Key postulates (ideal gas)

items: Molecules move randomly in straight lines between collisions.
Collisions are perfectly elastic; wall collisions cause pressure.
Average KE ∝ absolute temperature (same for all gases at one T).
Molecules' own volume is negligible; no attractions between them.

blocks.text: rms speed = √(3RT/M): lighter gas moves faster (H₂ is 4 × faster than O₂); 4 × T gives 2 × speed.
Real gases behave most ideally at LOW pressure and HIGH temperature. Easily liquefied gases (NH₃, SO₂, CO₂) deviate most; H₂ and He least.

title: Evaporation vs boiling, and vapour pressure

head: Feature
Evaporation
Boiling
rows: T stays constant while heat is supplied

blocks.text: Vapour pressure depends only on the nature of the liquid and its temperature, not on surface area or amount. Weaker intermolecular forces → higher vapour pressure → lower boiling point (ether > alcohol > water).

items: Murree (low pressure): water boils below 100 °C.
Pressure cooker (high pressure): water boils above 100 °C, food cooks faster.
Vacuum distillation: lower pressure lets heat-sensitive liquids boil below their decomposition point.

blocks.text: Surface area and wind change the RATE of evaporation, not the vapour pressure.

title: Hydrogen bonding and water's odd behaviour

blocks.text: Hydrogen bond: attraction between H bonded to F, O or N and a lone pair on another F, O or N. Weaker than a covalent bond, stronger than dipole forces (London < dipole–dipole < H-bond).

head: Compound
Boiling point
Why
rows: 2 H + 2 lone pairs → up to 4 H-bonds each
Strongest single H-bond, but fewer per molecule

items: Water is densest at 4 °C; it contracts from 0 to 4 °C, then expands.
Ice ≈ 0.92 g cm⁻³: open hydrogen-bonded cage, so ice floats and lakes freeze from the top (fish survive).
Water expands about 9% on freezing, so pipes burst.

blocks.text: NH₃ dissolves well in water because it forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules.

title: Crystal properties, ionic vs molecular crystals

blocks.text: Crystalline solids: regular repeating order, definite shape, sharp melting point, cleavage planes, anisotropic (properties differ with direction). Amorphous solids (glass, plastic) soften over a range and are isotropic.

items: Isomorphism: different substances, same crystal form (NaNO₃, CaCO₃).
Polymorphism: one substance, different crystal forms (calcite and aragonite).
Transition temperature: two forms coexist (rhombic ⇌ monoclinic sulphur, 95.5 °C).

title: Radius ratio, unit cell and lattice energy

blocks.text: Two key factors in ionic crystal shape: the radius ratio r⁺/r⁻ and the charges on the ions.
Unit cell: smallest repeating unit of the lattice; 7 crystal systems. Atoms per cell: simple cubic 1, face-centred cubic 4.
Lattice energy: energy released when 1 mole of ionic crystal forms from its gaseous ions, e.g. Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s). Found indirectly by the Born–Haber cycle.
Higher charges and smaller ions → larger lattice energy → higher melting point: MgO > NaCl > KCl; NaF > NaCl > NaBr > NaI.

title: Le Chatelier: which way it shifts

head: Change
Equilibrium shifts
Kc changes?
rows: To side with fewer gas moles
Pressure change, equal gas moles (H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI)

blocks.text: Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ. High pressure (about 200 atm) favours NH₃; a moderate 400–450 °C is a compromise between yield and rate; iron catalyst.
Only temperature changes the value of Kc.

title: Kc, Qc and Ksp in one sheet

items: Kc = [products]^coefficients ÷ [reactants]^coefficients; leave out pure solids and liquids.
Reverse the equation → new K = 1/Kc (Kc 50 → 0.02).
Units: (mol dm⁻³)^Δn, Δn = total coefficients of products − reactants in the Kc expression. Δn = 0 → no units; N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ → mol⁻² dm⁶.
Qc < Kc → goes forward; Qc > Kc → goes backward; Qc = Kc → at equilibrium.
Ksp from solubility s: AB → s²; AB₂ or A₂B (CaF₂, Ag₂CrO₄) → 4s³; A₃B₂ (Ca₃(PO₄)₂) → 108s⁵.
Precipitate forms when ionic product > Ksp.

blocks.text: Very large Kc (10³⁰) → mixture is almost all products. Same formula type: smaller Ksp = less soluble.
Common ion effect: adding an ion already present suppresses a weak electrolyte's ionisation or lowers a salt's solubility.

items: HCl gas into saturated NaCl → pure NaCl crystallises.
HCl with H₂S → low [S²⁻], so only group II sulphides precipitate.
NH₄Cl with NH₄OH → low [OH⁻], so only group III hydroxides precipitate.

head: Buffer
Made of
Example
rows: Weak acid + its salt with strong base
Weak base + its salt with strong acid

blocks.text: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]). Equal concentrations → pH = pKa (4.74 for acetic acid).
Strong acid + its salt (HCl + NaCl) is NOT a buffer.
Rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ. Overall order = m + n, found only by experiment, not from the balanced equation.
General unit of k: (mol dm⁻³)¹⁻ⁿ s⁻¹. Rate of a species ÷ its coefficient gives the rate of reaction. For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: NH₃ formed at 0.40 → rate of reaction 0.20 → H₂ used at 0.60 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
Order can be zero or a fraction; molecularity is always a whole number.

items: First order: t½ = 0.693/k, independent of starting concentration.
General: t½ ∝ 1/[A]₀ⁿ⁻¹ (zero order: t½ grows with [A]₀).
After n half-lives, fraction left = (½)ⁿ: 3 half-lives → 1/8.
0.80 → 0.10 in 60 min is three halvings, so t½ = 60 ÷ 3 = 20 min.
Rate-determining step = the slowest step; the rate law comes from it.
Pseudo-first order: one reactant in large excess (ester hydrolysis in water, sucrose inversion).

blocks.text: A species made in one step and used up in the next (like a free X atom) is an intermediate, not a catalyst.

items: Ea (forward) = peak energy − reactant energy.
Ea (reverse) = Ea (forward) − ΔH.
Exothermic: forward Ea < reverse Ea. Endothermic: forward Ea ≥ ΔH.
Activated complex sits at the peak: bonds partly broken, partly formed.
Catalyst lowers forward and reverse Ea by the same amount; ΔH, Kc and yield stay the same.
A 10 K rise roughly doubles the rate: more molecules have energy ≥ Ea (the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve flattens and shifts right).

blocks.text: Example: reactants 50, peak 150, products 20 kJ mol⁻¹ → Ea = 100, ΔH = −30, reverse Ea = 130.

Light (H₂ + Cl₂ explodes in sunlight) and surface area are rate factors too; temperature works mainly by raising the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea (Ea itself does not change), not by the small rise in collision count.

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: Change depends only on start and end

blocks.text: Reverse a reaction → same size ΔH, opposite sign. Photosynthesis is endothermic; respiration is exothermic.

items: ΔE = q + w (FSc convention: q = heat absorbed, w = work done ON the system).
Heat absorbed or work done on the system → +; heat lost or work done by the system → −.
Constant volume: ΔE = qv (bomb calorimeter). Constant pressure: ΔH = qp.
ΔH = ΔE + PΔV; ΔH ≈ ΔE when gas moles do not change (H₂ + I₂ → 2HI).
Work of expansion = PΔV: 100 kPa × 0.010 m³ = 1000 J.
1 J = 1 N m = 1 kg m² s⁻²; 1 cal = 4.184 J.

blocks.text: Absorbs 200 J, does 50 J of work → ΔE = 200 + (−50) = +150 J. Isolated system → ΔE = 0.
Total ΔH depends only on start and end, not on the route, because enthalpy is a state function.

items: Reverse an equation → change the sign of ΔH.
Multiply or halve an equation → do the same to ΔH.
Add the steps → add their ΔH values.
ΔH(reaction) = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants).
ΔHf of an element in its standard state = 0.

blocks.text: C + ½O₂ → CO: (C → CO₂, −394) minus (CO → CO₂, −283) = −111 kJ.
The Born–Haber cycle (lattice energy) is just Hess's law applied to an ionic solid.
OIL RIG
items: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons (oxidation number goes up)
Reduction Is Gain of electrons (oxidation number goes down)
Free element (O₂, P₄, S₈, Na) = 0; F is −1 in all its compounds.
O = −2, but −1 in peroxides (H₂O₂) and +2 in OF₂.
H = +1, but −1 in metal hydrides (NaH).
Sum = charge: S in H₂SO₄ +6, Mn in KMnO₄ +7, Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇ +6, N in NH₄⁺ −3, S in S₂O₃²⁻ +2.

blocks.text: The oxidising agent is itself reduced; the reducing agent is itself oxidised. Electrons lost = electrons gained.
Middle oxidation states (H₂O₂, SO₂) can act both ways; the lowest (H₂S, S = −2) can only reduce.

items: SHE: platinised Pt, H₂ at 1 atm, 1 M H⁺, 25 °C; E° = 0.00 V by convention.
More negative E° = stronger reducing agent (Li); more positive = stronger oxidising agent (F₂).
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode: Daniell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V; electrons flow Zn → Cu.
Metals with negative E° release H₂ from dilute acid; a lower-E° metal displaces a higher one.

blocks.text: AN OX, RED CAT: oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode, in every cell.
Repulsion: lone–lone > lone–bond > bond–bond, so each lone pair squeezes the angle (109.5 → 107 → 104.5).
SO₂ (2 bonding regions + 1 lone pair) is bent, not linear like CO₂.

items: Single bond = 1σ; double = 1σ + 1π; triple = 1σ + 2π.
Ethene 5σ 1π; ethyne 3σ 2π; benzene 12σ 3π; CO₂ 2σ 2π.
σ = head-on overlap (s–s, s–p, p–p or hybrid); π = sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals.
π is weaker than σ and stops free rotation about C=C.

blocks.text: More s character → shorter, stronger bond: C–H in ethyne is shortest. Propene CH₃–CH=CH₂ is sp³, sp², sp².
Symmetrical shape → bond dipoles cancel → zero dipole moment, even with polar bonds.

items: μ = 0: CO₂, BeCl₂, BF₃, CH₄, CCl₄, PCl₅, SF₆.
Polar: H₂O, NH₃, SO₂, CHCl₃, HCl (bent or pyramidal, or unequal atoms).
μ = charge × distance, unit debye (D). % ionic = observed μ ÷ 100%-ionic μ × 100 (1.2/6.0 → 20%).
Ionic character grows with electronegativity difference; about 1.7 ≈ 50% ionic. H–H, Cl–Cl have none.
Higher bond energy = stronger bond: C≡C > C=C > C–C; H–F > H–Cl > H–Br > H–I.

blocks.text: A polar XY₂ molecule must be bent; a linear one would have zero dipole moment.

items: IE dips: Mg > Al (3p¹ easy to remove) and N > O (paired 2p electron repels).
Highest electron affinity: Cl, not F (F is tiny and crowded).
Isoelectronic ions: more protons = smaller. O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺.
Covalent radius = half the bond length (Cl–Cl 198 pm → 99 pm).
Blocks: last electron in ns = s, np = p, (n−1)d = d, (n−2)f = f.

blocks.text: A big jump in successive IE marks a new inner shell: Na's 2nd IE is huge.

title: Group I and II metals: water and oxygen

blocks.text: Reactivity rises down both groups. With Cl₂: MCl and MCl₂; LiCl and BeCl₂ are the most covalent (BeCl₂ forms polymeric chains).
Diagonal pair Li–Mg: both form a nitride and a normal oxide only.

title: Group IV: oxidation states, chlorides, oxides

head: Element
Type
More stable state
Oxide nature
rows: CO₂ acidic (gas, small molecules); CO neutral

blocks.text: Inert pair effect: down the group the ns² pair is held more tightly and stays out of bonding, so +2 becomes more stable than +4.

items: CCl₄ is not hydrolysed: carbon has no vacant d orbitals for water to attack.
SiCl₄ + 4H₂O → Si(OH)₄ + 4HCl: Si uses vacant 3d orbitals.
PbCl₄ is the least stable tetrachloride: on gentle warming, PbCl₄ → PbCl₂ + Cl₂.

blocks.text: Oxides change from acidic to amphoteric down the group as metallic character rises. Catenation is greatest for carbon.

items: Exceptions: Cr = [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (half-full and full 3d are extra stable).
Making ions: 4s electrons leave FIRST, then 3d. Fe [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² → Fe²⁺ 3d⁶ → Fe³⁺ 3d⁵.
Highest oxidation state = 4s + 3d electrons, up to Mn (+7). Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇ is +6.
Sc shows only +3 (Sc³⁺ = [Ar]). Zn is not a typical transition element: Zn and Zn²⁺ both have full 3d¹⁰. Cu is one, because Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹.

blocks.text: First series: Sc (21) to Zn (30). General outer configuration (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻².
Variable oxidation states come from 4s and 3d being close in energy.
Spin-only formula: μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM. Fill the five 3d boxes singly before pairing (Hund's rule).
Most unpaired = 3d⁵ (5). Up to 3d⁵, n = number of d electrons; after it, n = 10 − d electrons.
Structural classes: open-chain (acyclic); closed-chain homocyclic (alicyclic e.g. cyclohexane, or aromatic e.g. benzene); heterocyclic, with N, O or S in the ring (pyridine N, furan O, thiophene S).
Same formula, different group = functional isomers: C₂H₆O ethanol vs methoxymethane; C₃H₆O propanal vs propanone.
Geometric (cis–trans)

items: Needs a C=C (no free rotation) AND two different groups on EACH double-bond carbon.
But-2-ene and ClCH=CHCl: yes. But-1-ene and propene (CH₂= end): no.
cis-1,2-dichloroethene is polar (higher b.p.); trans is non-polar (higher m.p.).

blocks.text: Optical

items: Needs a chiral carbon: four DIFFERENT groups, e.g. lactic acid CH₃CH(OH)COOH.
Enantiomers: non-superimposable mirror images; same physical properties except they rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions.
Racemic mixture: 50 : 50 of both, rotations cancel → optically inactive.

blocks.text: Count chiral C one by one: CH₃CH(OH)CH(Cl)CH₃ has two.

items: Initiation: Cl₂ —(UV / sunlight)→ 2Cl• (homolytic; Cl–Cl is weaker than C–H)
Propagation 1: Cl• + CH₄ → CH₃• + HCl
Propagation 2: CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• (Cl• regenerated → chain)
Termination: any two radicals join: Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂; CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl; CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆

blocks.text: Excess Cl₂ goes on: CH₃Cl → CH₂Cl₂ → CHCl₃ → CCl₄. Halogen reactivity: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. In the dark at room temperature: no reaction.
Traces of ethane (from methane) or butane (from ethane) prove CH₃• / C₂H₅• radicals joined in termination.
Making ethene (elimination)

items: C₂H₅OH —(conc. H₂SO₄, 170 °C; or Al₂O₃, 350 °C)→ CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O (at 140 °C with excess ethanol: diethyl ether)
C₂H₅Br + KOH —(alcoholic, heat)→ CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O

blocks.text: Reactions of CH₂=CH₂ (addition)

items: —(H₂, Ni, 200–300 °C)→ ethane
—(Br₂ in CCl₄, room temp)→ 1,2-dibromoethane (red-brown colour goes)
—(HBr)→ bromoethane; HI > HBr > HCl
—(cold conc. H₂SO₄, then boil with water)→ ethanol
—(cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄, Baeyer's)→ ethane-1,2-diol (pink goes)
—(O₃, then Zn/H₂O)→ 2 HCHO (methanal)
—(high pressure, heat, trace O₂)→ polythene

blocks.text: Markovnikov: propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane (H goes to the carbon that already has more H).
Steps: electrophile forms → attacks ring (slow) → arenium ion (one sp³ carbon) → loses H⁺ (fast), aromaticity restored.
o/p directors: –CH₃, –OH, –NH₂, halogens (but halogens deactivate). Meta directors: –NO₂, –CHO, –COOH, –CN, –SO₃H.
Above ~60 °C nitration also gives m-dinitrobenzene.

items: BrCH₂CH₂Br —(alcoholic KOH)→ CH₂=CHBr —(NaNH₂)→ HC≡CH (double dehydrohalogenation)
Br₂CHCHBr₂ —(Zn dust, heat)→ HC≡CH
HC≡CH —(H₂, Ni)→ ethene —(H₂, Ni)→ ethane
HC≡CH —(HBr)→ CH₂=CHBr —(HBr)→ CH₃CHBr₂ (1,1-dibromoethane, Markovnikov)
HC≡CH —(dil. H₂SO₄ + HgSO₄, 75 °C)→ [CH₂=CHOH, vinyl alcohol] → CH₃CHO; propyne gives propanone

blocks.text: Acidity of ≡C–H
sp carbon has 50% s character, so it holds electrons tightly: ethyne > ethene > ethane. Na → sodium acetylide + H₂; ammoniacal AgNO₃ → white ppt (Ag₂C₂); ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂ → red ppt (Cu₂C₂).
Only terminal alkynes give these precipitates: but-1-yne yes, but-2-yne no.
C–X carbon is δ+ and sp³, so nucleophiles attack it. Reactivity R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F: the weakest C–X bond breaks easiest, so I⁻ is the best leaving group.
Polarity is highest for C–F, but bond strength decides reactivity, not polarity.

title: Substitution or elimination? Read the solvent

items: Aqueous KOH / NaOH, warm → alcohol (substitution).
Alcoholic KOH, heat → alkene (elimination): H lost from the β-carbon, X from the α-carbon.
E2: one step, rate = k[RX][B⁻], strong base. E1: two steps via carbocation, rate = k[RX]; same slow step as SN1.
Elimination is favoured by a strong, concentrated base, alcoholic solvent, high temperature and a 3° halide.

blocks.text: (CH₃)₃CBr + hot alcoholic KOH → 2-methylpropene. 1-bromopropane and 2-bromopropane both give propene.
No β-hydrogen, no alkene: CH₃Br and (CH₃)₃CCH₂Br cannot eliminate.

items: ROH —Na→ RO⁻Na⁺ (alkoxide) + ½H₂ (gentler than Na + water)
ROH —PCl₅→ RCl + POCl₃ + HCl
ROH —SOCl₂ (pyridine)→ RCl + SO₂↑ + HCl↑
ROH —conc. H₂SO₄, ~180 °C→ alkene + H₂O
2ROH —conc. H₂SO₄, ~140 °C (excess alcohol)→ ROR (ether)
ROH + R′COOH —conc. H₂SO₄, warm⇌ R′COOR (ester) + H₂O
ROH + R′COCl —room temp→ ester + HCl (fast, not reversible)
RO⁻Na⁺ + R′X → ROR′ + NaX (Williamson ether synthesis)

blocks.text: 💡 SOCl₂ is preferred because both by-products are gases, leaving pure RCl.
⚠️ In esterification the acid loses –OH and the alcohol loses H, so ¹⁸O from the alcohol ends up in the ester, not in the water.
Example: propan-1-ol → propanal → propanoic acid; propan-2-ol → propanone; 2-methylpropan-2-ol is not oxidised.
💡 3° alcohols resist oxidation because the C bearing –OH has no H atom to lose.
⚠️ Iodoform (I₂ + NaOH → yellow CHI₃) is given by ethanol and by alcohols with CH₃CH(OH)– , not by methanol or propan-1-ol.

title: Phenol vs ethanol, and phenol's ring reactions

items: Br₂ water → 2,4,6-tribromophenol (3 Br₂ per phenol)
Br₂ in CS₂, low temp → 2- and 4-bromophenol
Dilute HNO₃ → 2- and 4-nitrophenol
Conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄ → 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid)

blocks.text: 💡 Acidity: RCOOH > phenol > water > ethanol. –OH activates the ring and directs ortho/para.

items: 1° alcohol —K₂Cr₂O₇ / dil. H₂SO₄, distil off at once→ aldehyde
2° alcohol —K₂Cr₂O₇ / dil. H₂SO₄→ ketone
Alkene —O₃, then Zn + H₂O→ aldehydes and/or ketones
Methanol vapour + air —hot Ag (or Cu) catalyst, ~500 °C→ methanal (industry)
Ethene + air —PdCl₂ / CuCl₂ in water→ ethanal (industry)

blocks.text: Ozonolysis examples: propene → methanal + ethanal; 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene → propanone only.
💡 Distilling the aldehyde off stops it being oxidised further to the carboxylic acid.
⚠️ Zn in ozonolysis removes H₂O₂, so the aldehyde is not oxidised to an acid.

items: + HCN (trace base, makes CN⁻) → cyanohydrin; then H₃O⁺, boil → 2-hydroxy acid
+ saturated NaHSO₃ → crystalline bisulphite adduct (aldehydes, methyl ketones)
+ 2,4-DNPH → orange/yellow 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone (addition then loss of H₂O)
+ NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ (H⁻), or H₂/Ni → aldehyde gives 1° alcohol, ketone gives 2° alcohol
Dilute NaOH, needs α-H → aldol (ethanal → 3-hydroxybutanal); heat → but-2-enal
Conc. NaOH, no α-H (HCHO, C₆H₅CHO) → Cannizzaro: alcohol + carboxylate salt

blocks.text: Reactivity: HCHO > CH₃CHO > CH₃COCH₃. Carbon goes sp² → sp³; nucleophile adds to C, H to O.
⚠️ LiAlH₄ reacts violently with water, so it is used in dry ether; NaBH₄ works in water or alcohol.
Tollens': aldehyde is oxidised to the acid (as its salt); Ag⁺ is reduced to Ag. 1 mol RCHO deposits 2 mol Ag (methanal, HCHO, can give 4 mol).
💡 Benzaldehyde: Tollens' positive, Fehling's negative. Propanal vs propanone: Tollens' or Fehling's. Ethanal vs propanal: iodoform.
⚠️ Methanal gives no iodoform. Strong oxidants split ketones into shorter acids.

title: Carboxylic acid map: make it, change it

items: RCH₂OH —K₂Cr₂O₇ / H⁺, reflux→ RCOOH
RX —KCN (ethanol)→ RCN —H₃O⁺, heat→ RCOOH (one C longer)
RMgX —CO₂, then H₃O⁺→ RCOOH (one C longer)

items: —SOCl₂→ RCOCl + SO₂↑ + HCl↑ ; —PCl₅→ RCOCl + POCl₃ + HCl
—R′OH, conc. H₂SO₄⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O
—NH₃→ RCOO⁻NH₄⁺ —heat→ RCONH₂ (amide) + H₂O

title: Acid strength and derivative reactivity orders

blocks.text: Acid strength
Cl₃CCOOH > Cl₂CHCOOH > ClCH₂COOH > HCOOH > CH₃COOH > C₆H₅OH > H₂O > C₂H₅OH

items: RCOO⁻ is resonance-stabilised: charge shared equally over two O atoms
Electron-withdrawing Cl (–I) strengthens the acid; more Cl, stronger
Alkyl groups (+I) weaken it, so HCOOH > CH₃COOH

blocks.text: Reactivity towards nucleophiles (e.g. water)
acyl chloride > anhydride > ester > amide
💡 Acyl chlorides fume in moist air (hydrolysis gives HCl) and give amides with NH₃ at room temperature.
⚠️ Ethanoic acid is weak: only partly ionised, so it conducts less than HCl of the same concentration.
